analysis.one_liner: Bans the manufacture, processing, and sale of asbestos and asbestos-containing products.
analysis.headline: The bill was introduced with 14 Senate supporters, sent to the Environment and Public Works Committee, and never received a hearing, a markup, or a vote before Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: Asbestos is a mineral fiber that causes cancers like mesothelioma decades after exposure. While dozens of countries have banned it, small amounts are still legally manufactured and imported in the United States. This bill would have made it illegal to make, process, or sell asbestos or products containing it one year after enactment, with narrow exemptions for national-security uses and no alternative available. It also required companies to report their recent asbestos activities to the EPA and required the EPA to study asbestos still sitting in older homes, schools, and public buildings.
analysis.who_benefits: Workers in chemical plants, refineries, shipyards, and auto repair shops, and their families, who are the people most likely to breathe asbestos fibers on the job. Ordinary residents benefit from removing a known carcinogen from commerce and from a government study of asbestos already in their homes, schools, and workplaces.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Workers and residents exposed to asbestos

how_it_helps.text: Prohibits the manufacture, processing, and distribution in commerce of asbestos or any mixture or article containing it, effective one year after enactment.

Requires anyone who made, processed, or distributed asbestos in the prior three years to report to the EPA the locations, quantities, uses, disposal methods, and estimated numbers of people exposed, and requires the EPA to make those reports public.

Directs the EPA, with the Health and Human Services and Labor Departments, to report within 540 days on how much asbestos remains in homes, schools, public, and commercial buildings, who is exposed, and what changes to law and regulation would reduce the risk.

Allows the President only narrow, temporary exemptions for national-security uses where no feasible alternative exists, capped at up to six years with published terms and public disclosure of applications.

analysis.who_pays: Companies that still manufacture or import asbestos — chiefly chlorine producers that use it in the chlor-alkali process and makers of certain brake, gasket, and other friction products — would have to stop or switch to substitutes, and bear the cost of new EPA reporting in the meantime.
analysis.who_pays_short: Chlorine producers and asbestos product importers

drawbacks.text: The ban exempts national-security uses, and allows the President to extend an exemption once for up to three more years, so the ban is not absolute and its scope depends on executive discretion.

The bill addresses new asbestos in commerce but does not mandate removal of asbestos already installed in buildings; it only requires a study and recommendations about that 'legacy' asbestos, so the largest exposure source for most people is deferred to later legislation.

The EPA's own risk evaluations were already examining the main ongoing uses, so industry groups argued a statutory ban would force costly substitutions of alternatives before replacements were fully proven for every application.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefit is straightforward: asbestos causes fatal cancers, and removing it from commerce eliminates new exposures at their source. The costs fall on a small number of industrial users who would need substitutes, and the bill softens that with a one-year phase-in and a narrow exemption. The main weakness is that the biggest existing exposure — asbestos already in walls, pipes, and ceilings — gets only a study, not action.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was read twice and referred to the Senate Environment and Public Works Committee the day it was introduced, and the committee never took it up before that Congress ended in January 2021.

narrative.text: Senator Jeff Merkley introduced the bill on March 7, 2019, with eleven original cosponsors listed on the introduced text.
It was read twice and referred to the Committee on Environment and Public Works on the day of introduction.
Fourteen senators total sponsored or cosponsored the bill — 13 Democrats and 1 Independent.
The action history shows no hearing, no committee vote, no floor action, and no roll call after the referral; the Congress ended January 3, 2021 without the bill moving.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: The companies still using and importing asbestos in the U.S. — chlorine makers and certain auto-parts suppliers — were better off, since the ban never took effect and they faced no new reporting or phase-out obligations during the 116th Congress.

for.name: Jeff Merkley
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and recruited cosponsors.

for.name: 13 Senate Democrats and 1 Independent
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill; none of them chaired a committee positioned to bring it to a vote.

against.name: John Barrasso
against.role: Chair, Senate Environment and Public Works Committee
against.what_they_did: As committee chair, never scheduled a hearing or markup on the bill, leaving it without any action for the full two-year Congress.

against.name: Chlor-alkali and asbestos-importing industries
against.role: Remaining U.S. commercial users of asbestos
against.what_they_did: Opposed a legislative ban and defended continued use of chrysotile asbestos in chlorine production, brakes, and gaskets.

sides.party_line_note: All 14 sponsors were Democrats or the Independent Bernie Sanders, no Senate Republicans cosponsored, and a Republican-run committee never acted on it.

industries.note: These producers are the main ongoing U.S. users of asbestos, which they use to make chlorine; a ban would force them onto substitute technology. Their interest in continuing to use asbestos runs against the public's interest in eliminating exposure to a carcinogen.

industries.industry: Asbestos product importers (brakes, gaskets, friction products)
industries.note: Importers and makers of asbestos-containing auto and industrial parts would have to stop within a year. Continued sales of these products mean continued workplace exposure for mechanics and factory workers.

The EPA legacy-asbestos study and any follow-on inspection or removal programs would create work for firms that survey, contain, and remove asbestos. The public benefit and this industry's gain point the same way.
